questions.title: CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier vs Semaphore
questions.question: What are the differences between CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, and Semaphore, and when do you use each?
questions.direct_answer: CountDownLatch is a one-shot countdown that lets one or more threads wait until N operations complete. CyclicBarrier is a reusable rendezvous point where N threads all wait for each other before any proceeds. Semaphore controls access to a pool of N permits, making it suitable for rate-limiting or bounded resource pools.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to match the right coordination primitive to a problem rather than always reaching for synchronized.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing CountDownLatch (cannot be reset) with CyclicBarrier (can be reset and reused), leading to incorrect designs for iterative parallel algorithms.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that Phaser (Java 7+) generalises both CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier with dynamic party registration and multiple phases.

sections.title: Latch Is One-Shot, Barrier Is Reusable, Semaphore Is a Permit Pool — Three Different Coordination Problems
sections.content:
These three synchronizers solve fundamentally different coordination problems, and confusing them is one of the most common interview mistakes.

**CountDownLatch** is a one-shot gate. Initialize with a count N, then threads call `await()` to block until the count reaches zero. Other threads call `countDown()` to decrement.

Once zero, the latch **opens permanently** — subsequent `await()` calls return immediately and it cannot be reset.

Use case: main thread waits for N worker threads to complete initialization before starting the application. Or: N workers wait for a start signal from the coordinator.

**CyclicBarrier** is a reusable meeting point. N threads call `await()` and block until all N have arrived. Then all are released simultaneously, and the barrier **resets for the next cycle**. Optionally runs a barrier action when the last thread arrives.

Use case: iterative algorithms where all threads must complete phase K before any thread starts phase K+1. Matrix computation, simulation steps.

**Semaphore** is a permit pool. Initialize with N permits. `acquire()` takes a permit (blocks if none available). `release()` returns a permit. Unlike locks, the thread that releases does not have to be the thread that acquired.

Use case: rate limiting, connection pooling, limiting concurrent access to a resource. `Semaphore(1)` is a binary semaphore — functionally similar to a mutex but lacking reentrancy and ownership tracking.

sections.title: Coordination Pattern, Reusability, and Thread Behavior
sections.content:
The table clarifies which synchronizer matches which coordination pattern.

| Feature | CountDownLatch | CyclicBarrier | Semaphore |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Wait for N events | Wait for N threads to arrive | Limit concurrent access to N permits |
| Reusable | No — one-shot, cannot reset | Yes — resets after all threads arrive | Yes — permits returned via release() |
| Who decrements/releases | Any thread (countDown) | The arriving threads (await) | Any thread (release) |
| Blocks until | Count reaches zero | All parties arrive | A permit is available |
| Broken/timeout handling | No broken state | BrokenBarrierException if one thread fails | No broken state |
| Typical thread count | Waiters and counters can be different | All threads must participate | Any number of threads |

The **reusability** row is the key differentiator between Latch and Barrier. A latch counts events (which may come from any source). A barrier counts thread arrivals (all participating threads must arrive before any proceeds).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`CountDownLatch`** — one-shot gate; count from N to 0; all waiting threads proceed; cannot be reset.
- **`CyclicBarrier`** — reusable meeting point; N threads all block until everyone arrives; barrier resets; one failure = BrokenBarrierException.
- **`Semaphore`** — permit pool; `acquire()` takes, `release()` returns; any thread can release (unlike a mutex).
- **`Semaphore(1)` is NOT a mutex** — lacks reentrancy; a thread acquiring twice deadlocks itself.
- **Choose by problem** — Latch for one-time waits, Barrier for phased algorithms, Semaphore for resource limiting.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, and Semaphore solve three different coordination problems — one-time gates, reusable meeting points, and permit pools.

**CountDownLatch:**
- One-shot gate: count down from N; when zero, all waiting threads proceed; cannot be reset
- Use for: waiting until N services initialize, waiting for N subtasks to complete

**CyclicBarrier:**
- Reusable meeting point: N threads call `await()`, all block until everyone arrives, all proceed together, barrier resets automatically
- Use for: phased computations where all threads must finish step K before starting step K+1
- If one thread fails: barrier breaks, all others get `BrokenBarrierException`

**Semaphore:**
- Permit pool: `acquire()` takes a permit (blocks if none available), `release()` returns one
- Any thread can release — not just the acquirer (unlike a mutex)
- Use for: rate limiting, connection pooling
- `Semaphore(1)` is not a true mutex — lacks reentrancy; a thread acquiring twice deadlocks itself

I recommend Latch for one-time initialization waits, Barrier for iterative parallel algorithms, and Semaphore for resource access limiting.

questions.title: ThreadLocal — Use Cases and Pitfalls
questions.question: What is ThreadLocal in Java, when should you use it, and what are its main pitfalls?
questions.direct_answer: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own independent copy of a variable, eliminating the need for synchronisation when each thread needs isolated state. Common uses include per-thread database connections, request-scoped context (like user identity in a web request), and SimpleDateFormat instances. The primary pitfall is memory leaks in thread pools: if the ThreadLocal is not explicitly removed, the value outlives the logical request and accumulates across reuses of the same thread.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of thread-scoped state management and the lifecycle responsibility that comes with ThreadLocal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not calling remove() at the end of a request, leading to stale data leaking into subsequent requests handled by the same pooled thread.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Java 20+ ScopedValue (JEP 429) is the preferred replacement for ThreadLocal in virtual-thread-heavy code because it is immutable and does not leak across thread boundaries.

sections.title: ThreadLocal Gives Each Thread Its Own Copy — But Thread Pools Turn That Feature Into a Memory Leak
sections.content:
ThreadLocal provides **per-thread isolated storage** — each thread has its own independent copy of the variable, invisible to other threads. No synchronization needed because there is no sharing. This is ideal for per-thread state like database connections, date formatters (pre-Java 8), or transaction contexts.

The mechanism is simple: each `Thread` object has a `ThreadLocal.ThreadLocalMap` — a hash map keyed by `ThreadLocal` instances. `threadLocal.get()` looks up the value in the current thread's map. `threadLocal.set(value)` stores it. The map is private to the thread, so no other thread can access it.

The **memory leak** happens with thread pools. In a pool, threads are reused — they do not terminate. If a task sets a ThreadLocal value and does not call `remove()`, the value persists for the lifetime of the thread. Over thousands of requests, this accumulates objects that are never collected.

In web applications, this is especially dangerous. A request sets a ThreadLocal with user context. The next request on the same thread sees the **previous user's context** if `remove()` was not called — a security vulnerability on top of the memory leak.

Java 20 introduced **ScopedValue** as a replacement for many ThreadLocal use cases — it provides structured, bounded scoping that automatically cleans up when the scope exits.

sections.title: The Memory Leak Mechanism and the remove() Discipline
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Each thread gets its own copy** — `ThreadLocalMap` keyed by ThreadLocal; `get()` always returns the calling thread's copy.
- **Thread pool trap** — pool threads are reused; without `remove()`, the value leaks across requests.
- **Security issue** — next request on that thread sees the previous user's context data.
- **Fix: try-finally with `remove()`** — mandatory in any pooled environment: Tomcat, Spring, ExecutorService.
- **`InheritableThreadLocal` doesn't work with pools** — pool threads aren't children of the submitting thread.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
ThreadLocal gives each thread its own isolated copy of a variable — no synchronization needed because there is no sharing.

**How it works:**
- Each `Thread` object has a private `ThreadLocalMap` keyed by `ThreadLocal` instances
- `get()` always returns the calling thread's own copy; `set()` writes only to that thread's map

**Thread pool trap:**
- Pool threads are reused, not terminated — if a task sets a ThreadLocal without calling `remove()`, the value persists for the thread's lifetime
- Memory leak: accumulates stale values across thousands of requests
- Security issue: next request on that thread sees the previous user's context data — dangerous for user-scoped state

**Fix — try-finally pattern:**
- Set the ThreadLocal, do the work, call `remove()` in `finally` — mandatory in any pooled environment
- Tomcat, Spring, and ExecutorService all reuse threads

**InheritableThreadLocal:**
- Copies values to child threads at creation — does not work with pools, since pool threads are not children of the submitting thread

I recommend minimizing ThreadLocal usage in modern Java. ScopedValue (Java 20) provides structured scoping with automatic cleanup and is the preferred replacement for request-scoped context.
